title: E-commerce photo studio: how to set it up for your in-house packshots?
h1: E-commerce photo studio: organizing reliable image production
metaTitle: How do you organize an in-house e-commerce photo studio? | Orbitvu & PackshotCreator
description: Discover how to structure your in-house e-commerce photo studio with Orbitvu and PackshotCreator. Automation, AI, and efficient organization to produce professional visuals on your own.
author: PackshotCreator
content:
Article updated on October 14, 2026.

A well-equipped studio is not enough to produce the right images, under the right name, on time. Reliability comes down to organization: who decides what, how each image stays attached to its product, how a look can be reproduced months later, and how you check what goes online.

Here are eight questions, in the order of the production flow. They assume the decision has been made; if it has not, start with article 1 of this series.

Series · Producing your product images

  1. 1Decide Before setting up an e-commerce photo studio: the questions to ask yourself
  2. 2Produce E-commerce photo studio: organizing reliable image production

Who should be responsible for each step?

In brief

One named person for each step, and only one for each decision. In a small team, the same person plays several roles; what matters is that every decision has an identified owner.

To go further, organizing the studio, as seen by Sébastien Jourdan complements these organizational benchmarks.

Who does what, and who decides
RoleResponsible forDecides
RequestThe brief: references, variants, views, channels, go-live dateWhat must be produced
Receiving and preparationIdentifying the sample and preparing itWhether the sample matches the product sheet
ShootingThe shooting template, the sequence, the first checkWhether the image is technically usable
Processing and filesClipping, retouching, export by channelWhether the files comply with the channels
Product validationComparison with the real productWhether the image shows the product being sold
Brand validationThe look and the brand guidelinesWhether the image follows the brand guidelines
PublicationGoing live and checking on the channelWhen the image goes out

These roles detail those described in the first version of this article: project manager, photographer, assistant, editor. The titles matter less than the rule: one decision, one owner.

Points to check
  • Who makes the call when marketing and product validation disagree?
  • Who can stop a series in progress if the first product does not comply?
  • Who updates the shooting templates, and who is informed?
  • Who stands in for each owner during absences?

How do you tie each image to the right SKU and variant?

In brief

With a single pivot identifier, the product code your systems already use (GTIN, EAN or internal reference), carried from the moment the sample is received to the export, and a file name derived from that code, with no free-text entry.

Every manual handover is a chance for error. Sébastien Jourdan writes this about a chain where photography, measurement and data entry take place at three separate workstations: “Three workstations. Three handling steps. At every transfer, a chance to make a mistake, and time lost.” An image attached to the wrong item means a wrong product page.

The GS1 product image standard (GS1 Product Image Standard, version 5.0) proposes a convention: the 14 digits of the GTIN, an underscore, then letters and digits that encode, among other things, the image type, the face shown, the angle and the state of the product, packaged or not. GS1 specifies that these file names are not GS1 identifiers.

See the method in practice
  1. At receiving: scan or enter the sample’s code, and check that it matches the product sheet to be illustrated (right variant, right color, right packaging).
  2. At the shoot: have the software derive the file name from the product code, with no free-text entry.
  3. In the name: add the variant and the view, in a fixed order.
  4. When returning to stock: relabel the sample if it has been unpacked.

A color that has not been photographed does not get another color’s file renamed. If it is produced by recoloring, it follows the check described in question 8.

How do you reproduce the same look months later?

In brief

By writing a shooting guide, saving one shooting template per product family, and keeping for each family a dated reference image against which to compare new ones.

On listing pages, the Nielsen Norman Group recommends consistent photos: same background, same lighting, same scale. Restocks and new colors, photographed months later and sometimes by someone else, must blend in with the images already online without a visible break.

“Shooting templates stay within the company: the next collection is photographed under the same conditions as the previous one, even if the operator changes.”

PackshotCreator, “Packshot mode” page, October 1, 2026
Main view
The GS1 standard favors a front view with a 15° elevation, then rotations of 15° to the left and right; 0° for flat products.
Framing
GS1: the product fills about 80% of the sensor at capture.
Background, margins, shadow
Set once and for all, then applied by the export.
Lighting
One template per family of materials, “tested on a representative piece” (Packshot mode page).

Inherited settings are a trap. About a change of equipment, Sébastien Jourdan asks: “How many inherited settings survive only because nobody dares touch them anymore?” Reviewing the templates at every equipment change, and at least once a year, avoids repeating old mistakes.

See the method in practice

For each family, a short sheet is enough:

  • the name of the shooting template;
  • the reference product, kept if possible;
  • the reference image, dated;
  • the settings: lighting, camera, angles, background, margins;
  • the owner and the date of the last review.

What can be automated, and what is left to do by hand?

In brief

You automate the repetition: recalling settings, view sequence, clipping, cropping, format variants, export. What stays manual is handling the product and exercising judgment: unpacking, cleaning, shaping, positioning, checking the tricky cases.

Sébastien Jourdan’s experience

“The studio automates this sequence according to the configured profiles: clipping, cropping, size and format variants, then export to a local folder, a server or a compatible online store. The operator keeps control of the result, particularly on delicate products.”

Sébastien Jourdan, photographer and president of Sysnext (PackshotCreator), field benchmarks published on the e-commerce Packshot page, September 28, 2026

Upstream, the gesture remains human: “Unpacking, dusting, smoothing out creases or shaping a product remains manual work.” For products from the same family, the same benchmarks describe a precise sequence: the operator recalls the saved configuration, positions the product for the first view, launches the sequence, and prepares the next product while the studio runs through the angles.

No studio, on the other hand, automates:

  • the quality of upstream data (see the question “tie each image to the right SKU”);
  • requests that change after the session (see the question “avoid reshoots”);
  • the choice of what must be produced;
  • the final comparison with the real product (see the question “check image fidelity”).

The detail of the steps, automatic or manual, is in the table on the e-commerce Packshot page.

How do you handle difficult materials, reflections and transparencies?

In brief

Family by family: a dedicated lighting template, one setting per view for shiny products, tested on the most difficult piece, and deliberate manual retouching on tricky cases rather than automatic processing that fails without warning.

Sébastien Jourdan’s experience

Why the same product needs one setting per view:

“A watch, for example, can be perfectly lit from the front. Switch to a three-quarter view without changing the lighting: a reflection appears on the dial and hides the details you wanted to show.”

Sébastien Jourdan, photographer and president of Sysnext (PackshotCreator), field benchmarks published on the e-commerce Packshot page, September 28, 2026

Soft materials raise the same question. PackshotCreator writes this about textiles: “A knit, a denim, a velvet or a satin do not react to light in the same way. Lighting set to bring out the grain of a matte fabric can make a satin fabric shine.”

Reflections
Polished metal, watch crystal, varnish: one saved setting per view, and a check of every angle, not just the front.
Transparencies
Glass, bottles: the background can be removed at capture on backlit studios, or by AI in the software; the outlines are checked on screen.
Fine elements
Chains, threads, frames: automatic clipping is checked image by image on these families.
Small objects
Jewelry, technical parts: focus stacking keeps the product sharp throughout its depth.
Difficult colors
Blacks, whites, saturated colors: they are checked on screen, by comparing the image with the piece.

For shadow, version 26.2 of the Orbitvu Station software, released on June 23, 2026, clips during capture “with the option to keep the product’s natural shadow,” as Sébastien Jourdan describes in his article on migrating older studios (read the article).

Points to check

For each difficult family:

  • the reference piece on which the template was tested;
  • the setting saved for each view;
  • the manual retouching that is allowed, and the kind that is not;
  • the on-screen check against the product, before the series.

How do you avoid endless approvals and reshoots?

In brief

A single channel for requests, a brief set before the session, validation on the first product of a family rather than image by image, and two separate decisions: conformity to the product and brand look.

The minimum brief, per product or per batch:

  • the reference and the variant;
  • the expected views;
  • the distribution channels;
  • the go-live date;
  • the product’s constraints: fragile, shiny, needs assembly.

A request changed after the session becomes a reshoot. Record it as such, with its cause.

Validate the template, not every image. Validation applies to the first product of a family, that is, to the shooting template; the series follows if the template is validated. Conformity to the product and brand look do not fall to the same people: separate them, with one owner each (see the question “Who is responsible for each step”).

See the method in practice

A reshoot never overwrites the original image. Keep the date and the cause of each reshoot, classified in one of these categories:

  • sample: wrong product, wrong variant, damaged product;
  • shooting template: lighting, angle, framing;
  • export: name, dimensions, margins, background;
  • data: wrong reference or variant;
  • request changed after the session.

A recurring cause is fixed in the template or in the export, not image by image.

How do you automatically deliver the right files to each channel?

In brief

One master file per view, one export profile per channel (format, dimensions, margins, naming) and a test delivery per channel before mass production.

The export profile does the repetitive work. Sébastien Jourdan describes it for the Orbitvu Station shooting software: its publication profiles “set the format, resolution and naming of each output.”

For the master file, the GS1 standard recommends storing in TIFF with LZW compression, and sharing in JPEG or PNG. Platform requirements, for their part, change: check them at the time of publication. The dated table of the main requirements is on the e-commerce Packshot page.

Then test a real delivery on each channel and check the image as displayed, zoom included. The Baymard Institute found insufficient image resolution or zoom on 25% of the sites it evaluated.

See the method in practice

An export profile can be described in eight lines:

  • the profile name and the target channel;
  • the format and compression;
  • the dimensions and the aspect ratio;
  • the margins and the position of the product;
  • the background;
  • the color space required by the channel;
  • the naming rule;
  • the destination: folder, server or online store.

Read also JPEG, PNG, RAW, WebP: which image format for the web

How do you check image fidelity, including after AI processing?

In brief

By checking according to risk, and by comparing every retouched, recolored or generated image with the real photo of the product: shape and proportions, text and logos, color and material, added elements.

Three levels of checking
LevelWhatHow
Automatic, on 100% of filesName, match with the reference, dimensions, format, background, marginsExport rules and file checks
Targeted visual checkFirst product of each family; glass, reflections, fine elements; difficult colors; any image modified by AIComparison with the real product or its reference photo
SamplingThe other imagesRate set according to the errors observed

The nature of the risk changes depending on what the AI does. When it works on the photo, “this AI works on a real photo of the real product,” writes Sébastien Jourdan about the tools built into the shooting software. When it generates a background, a staging, a color or a missing view, it can alter the product: models that generate a background around a product tend to extend its outlines and change its identity (Eshratifar et al., 2024).

“The real photo of each piece serves as the reference: taken in the studio, it then feeds the AI-assisted uses. Every derived image is compared with this reference before being published.”

PackshotCreator, “Packshot mode” page, October 1, 2026

Compare four points:

  • the shape and proportions;
  • the text, logos and patterns;
  • the color and material;
  • added elements that suggest content that is not delivered.

Recoloring follows the same rule: PackshotCreator regards it as “a stopgap, not a rule,” because “a recolored image is not a photo of the real color.”

Points to check
  • Metadata: Google Merchant Center requires images created by generative AI to be flagged with the IPTC Digital Source Type property, and asks that this metadata not be removed.
  • Platform checks: Zalando describes an engine that automatically compares generated content with the product’s original images and flags discrepancies.
  • The European framework: according to the European Commission’s guidelines on Article 50 of the AI Act, which are non-binding, removing a background that is visible in the original file counts as standard formatting.

Production checklist

Organization

  • Every step has a named owner; every decision, a single person.
  • Requests arrive through a single channel, with a minimum brief set before the session.

Identification

  • A single pivot identifier follows the sample, from receiving to export.
  • The file name is derived from the product code, with the variant and the view, with no free-text entry.

Consistency

  • A written guide sets background, angles, framing, margins and shadow.
  • Each family has its shooting template and a dated reference image.
  • Templates are reviewed at every equipment change, and at least once a year.

Automation

  • Settings, view sequence, clipping and export are recalled automatically.
  • Tricky cases are listed, with the manual retouching that is allowed.

Distribution

  • A master file is kept for each view.
  • Each channel has its export profile, tested with a real delivery.

Checking

  • Measurable checks are automatic; the visual check targets delicate families and products.
  • Every image modified or generated by AI is compared with the real photo.
  • Reshoots are recorded with their cause, without overwriting the original image.
